A course you read, not watch

Most courses on this platform use video as their main format. This one doesn't. Introduction to Psychology is built almost entirely around reading — and that isn't an accident or a limitation: it's how you actually learn this discipline.

Psychology isn't a collection of "mind-reading tips" or motivational social media quotes. It's a science with more than a century of experiments, debates and discoveries, and understanding it seriously takes the same kind of effort you'd put into any science: reading carefully, questioning, and going back over what wasn't clear.

💡 How to read a class in this course well:
  1. Read the whole module once, without stopping to take notes.
  2. Read it again slowly, and this time underline or note (mentally or in a notebook) what surprised you or what you didn't understand.
  3. Before moving to "Next class," answer the reflection quest with your pet — explaining something in your own words is the best way to know if you truly understood it.

The course map

We're going to cover psychology in the same order most university textbooks present it:

  • Fundamentals (classes 2-5): what psychology is, its history, its major schools of thought, and how science is done on the mind.
  • Basic processes (classes 6-9): the brain, how we learn, how we remember (and forget), and what emotions are.
  • The person and others (classes 10-12): personality, development across the lifespan, and social psychology — how being around other people changes us.
  • Wrap-up (class 13): your own mind map of everything you learned, and where to keep reading if this hooked you.
📖 An honest heads-up: you're going to run into names like Freud, Skinner or Milgram. Part of thinking like a scientist is learning to admire someone's historical contribution without accepting all of their ideas uncritically — that's also psychology, and you're going to practice it in this course.

1f79c9cdbb27be:
A surprising definition

Psychology is defined as the science that studies the mind and behavior. It's a short definition, but every word carries weight: it's a science (based on evidence, not opinion), it studies the mind (thoughts, emotions, perception) and behavior (what can be observed from the outside).

Psychology's 4 goals

Every psychologist, no matter their specialty, pursues four goals:

  1. Describe: observe and record behavior precisely (what exactly is happening?).
  2. Explain: understand why it happens (what causes this behavior?).
  3. Predict: anticipate when it will happen again (under what conditions does it repeat?).
  4. Change: intervene to modify it when needed (therapy, education, public policy).
❌ Common myth: "the psychologist reads your mind" or "analyzes you just by looking at you." That doesn't exist — not even clinical psychologists with years of experience can "guess" a person without listening to them and assessing them with real tools.

Psychology vs. self-help vs. common sense

Not every claim about the human mind is "psychology." A motivational quote on social media can sound true and have no backing at all. Common sense, too, is often wrong: for decades it was "known" that physical punishment taught discipline, until the evidence showed the opposite.

💡 Your filter for the rest of the course: every time you read a psychological claim (here or anywhere else), ask yourself: was this tested with some method, or is it just an idea that sounds good?

161b055e59091a:
Five lenses for looking at the same mind

Throughout the 20th century several "schools" emerged, competing to explain human behavior. None of them had the whole picture — but each left behind ideas that are still alive today.

1. 🛋️ Psychoanalysis (Sigmund Freud)

Proposed that much of our behavior is guided by unconscious processes — desires and conflicts we don't see but that drive us. Ideas like "defense mechanism" come from here.

⚠️ Critical note: many of Freud's specific ideas (like the "Oedipus complex") don't hold up against modern evidence and are today considered more history than active science. His real contribution was opening up the idea that not everything in the mind is conscious — something modern neuroscience does confirm.

2. 🐕 Behaviorism (John Watson, B.F. Skinner)

Rejected studying "what can't be seen" (thoughts, emotions) and focused only on observable behavior and how it's learned through conditioning (you'll see this in class 7). Very influential in education and therapy.

3. 🌱 Humanism (Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers)

A reaction against behaviorism's "cold" view. Put human potential, self-actualization and therapeutic empathy at the center. Maslow's famous "hierarchy of needs" comes from here.

4. 🧩 Cognitive psychology

Starting in the 1960s, the mind's "inner workings" started being studied again — but with scientific method: memory, attention, decision-making, comparing the mind to a system that processes information.

5. 🧬 Biological perspective / neuroscience

Studies how the brain, genes and body chemistry produce thoughts, emotions and behavior. Today it's, along with the cognitive approach, the dominant force in research.

💡 Modern psychology doesn't pick just one school — it combines pieces from all of them depending on the question being researched. That's what you'll see in the rest of the course.

13b33addb9a7a4:
How do you "prove" something about the mind?

When a psychologist says "stress affects memory," that sentence didn't come from intuition — it came from studies designed to test (or disprove) that idea. There are two main tools:

Correlational studies

Measure whether two variables move together (for example, hours of sleep and academic performance) without manipulating anything. They're useful, but have a huge limit: correlation does not imply causation. Two things happening together doesn't prove one causes the other.

Experiments

Here a variable (the "independent variable") IS manipulated to see its effect on another (the "dependent variable"), comparing an experimental group against a control group. It's the only way to establish causation with confidence.

📝 Example: to find out if sleeping well IMPROVES memory (not just relates to it), an experiment would randomly assign one group to sleep 8 hours and another to sleep 4, then test both with the same memory test.

When science crossed the line

Psychology has an uncomfortable history with ethics. The Milgram experiment (1961) led participants to believe they were delivering painful electric shocks to another person just to obey an authority figure — and most of them did. The Stanford Prison Experiment (1971) assigned "guard" and "prisoner" roles to students and had to be cancelled because of the level of real abuse that emerged.

⚠️ Both studies revealed uncomfortable truths about obedience and the power of a situation — but they also caused real psychological harm to their participants. That's why today EVERY study with humans goes through an ethics committee that requires informed consent and protection for participants.

0bec651fe788fa: Neurons, neurotransmitters and the brain's basic regions — the biological foundation for everything you think, feel and do.
0b9580791fab95:
It all starts with one cell

Every thought, emotion or movement you have is, at bottom, electrical and chemical activity in your brain. The basic unit of this system is the neuron: a cell specialized in receiving and transmitting signals.

Neurons don't touch each other — they communicate across a tiny gap called the synapse, releasing chemical substances called neurotransmitters.

🧪 Some key neurotransmitters:
  • Dopamine: motivation, reward, pleasure.
  • Serotonin: mood, emotional regulation.
  • Cortisol (a hormone, not a neurotransmitter): stress response.
  • Oxytocin: social bonding and trust.

A very simplified map of the brain

  • Prefrontal cortex: planning, decision-making, impulse control. It's one of the last areas to mature (until about age 25).
  • Amygdala: processing fear and intense emotions.
  • Hippocampus: forming new memories (key for class 8).
  • Cerebellum: motor coordination and balance.
💡 Why it matters: knowing the prefrontal cortex doesn't finish maturing until about age 25 explains (without excusing) why teenagers tend to take more risks — the part of the brain that "brakes" impulses is still under construction.
❌ Common myth: "we only use 10% of the brain." False — neuroimaging studies show activity spread across practically the whole brain, even in simple tasks.

1d02e254196922: Pavlov and his dogs, Skinner and his boxes: the two most-studied learning mechanisms in psychology, and how they act in your daily life without you noticing.
1b4ce31d6dcbad:
Classical conditioning: learning by association

Ivan Pavlov, studying digestion in dogs, noticed something unexpected: his dogs began salivating just from hearing the footsteps of the assistant who brought the food — before even seeing the food. Learning by association had occurred.

📝 The experiment: Pavlov rang a bell (neutral stimulus) right before giving food (a stimulus that naturally triggers salivation). After several repetitions, the bell ALONE already triggered salivation — a new association had been "conditioned."

This explains everyday phenomena: if a particular piece of music plays every time you go to the dentist, that music alone can later trigger anxiety, even though there's nothing wrong with it on its own.

Operant conditioning: learning by consequences

B.F. Skinner took the idea further: behavior gets stronger or weaker depending on its consequences.

  • Positive reinforcement: adding something pleasant to increase a behavior (giving candy for good behavior).
  • Negative reinforcement: removing something unpleasant to increase a behavior (turning off an annoying alarm when you get up).
  • Punishment: adding something unpleasant (or removing something pleasant) to DECREASE a behavior.
⚠️ Punishment suppresses a behavior in the short term, but the evidence shows positive reinforcement tends to produce longer-lasting learning with fewer side effects (fear, resentment). That's why modern education prioritizes reinforcing the good over punishing the bad.
💡 See it in your own life: your phone's notifications, "likes" on social media, and this very educational platform's point systems use operant conditioning principles — reinforcement (a reward) makes you want to repeat the behavior (opening the app again, continuing to learn).

072767370c78bf: The three stages of memory, why we forget so fast what we don't review, and real (evidence-based) tricks for remembering better.
0d9f21c7b58c04:
Memory isn't a recorder

One of the most common myths is thinking memory works like a camera that records everything perfectly. In reality, it's an active, reconstructive process — every time you remember something, you kind of "rewrite" it, which makes it vulnerable to errors.

Three stages of the process

  1. Encoding: transforming the information you perceive into a form the brain can store.
  2. Storage: keeping that information over time (short-term vs. long-term memory).
  3. Retrieval: bringing that information back when you need it — this is where we tend to fail the most.

The forgetting curve

Psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus discovered we forget most of what we learn within the first hours and days if we don't review it — and that each review spaced out over time makes the forgetting curve slower and slower.

💡 Apply it right now: if you want to remember what you read in this course a month from now, reading it once isn't enough. Go back and review earlier modules every so often — it's the technique with the most scientific evidence for durable learning, called "spaced repetition."
📝 Why the reflection with your pet actually helps: explaining something in your own words forces your brain to actively "retrieve" the information, not just recognize it — and active retrieval strengthens memory much more than passively rereading.
❌ Myth: "repressed" memories come back intact through hypnosis or therapy. The evidence shows memories "recovered" under suggestion can actually be false memories, built without us realizing it.

041f43f87579fa: Emotions: what they are and what they're for
0a2f5bb96224f2: Emotions aren't "noise" that interferes with clear thinking — they're an information system that evolved to help you survive and decide.
0d5b8bfaf840ec:
Emotions have a function

For a long time, emotions were thought to be the opposite of reason — "noise" that had to be controlled to think clearly. Modern psychology sees emotions differently: as fast information signals about what's happening, useful for deciding and acting quickly.

📝 Example: fear at a sudden loud noise makes you react (duck, move away) before your conscious thought even finishes analyzing whether there's real danger. That speed, over evolutionary history, saved lives.

How many "basic" emotions are there?

Psychologist Paul Ekman proposed that there are basic emotions universally recognizable by their facial expression, regardless of culture: joy, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust. The rest of the emotions we feel would be combinations or more nuanced variants of these.

Emotional regulation

Feeling an emotion isn't the problem — what we do with it can be. Emotional regulation is the ability to recognize, understand and manage an emotion without it completely controlling you.

💡 A real technique, not generic self-help: naming what you feel ("I'm feeling frustration, not just anger") measurably reduces the intensity of the emotional reaction in the brain — this phenomenon is called "affect labeling" and does have neuroimaging study support.
⚠️ Systematically repressing an emotion (pretending you don't feel it) doesn't eliminate it — the evidence shows it tends to increase physiological stress in the long run. Regulating isn't the same as repressing.

1b68457815a231: The "Big Five" personality trait model, and the eternal debate: are we born this way, or do we become this way?
1567705f4b08a4:
Can personality be measured?

Personality is the relatively stable patterns of thinking, feeling and behaving that set you apart from other people. For decades, different psychologists proposed extremely long lists of "traits" — until statistical analysis of thousands of studies reduced them to the model with the most support today: the Big Five.

📝 The five traits (English acronym: OCEAN):
  • Openness to experience: curiosity, creativity, enjoying new things.
  • Conscientiousness: organization, discipline, goal orientation.
  • Extraversion: sociability, energy, seeking external stimulation.
  • Agreeableness: cooperation, empathy, trust in others.
  • Neuroticism: tendency to experience negative emotions more intensely.

A person doesn't "have" or "not have" a trait — they fall somewhere on a continuous spectrum on each of the five. That's why serious personality tests give results as percentages or levels, not rigid categories like "type A" or "type B."

Nature or nurture?

Studies with identical twins raised apart show that roughly 40-60% of the variation in personality traits has a genetic component — the rest is explained by environment, experiences and life choices.

❌ Myth: "16 personalities" tests like MBTI (popularized online) don't have the same scientific backing as the Big Five model — they're entertaining, but don't hold up the same way under rigorous statistical review.
💡 Personality isn't 100% fixed: it changes (a little, but really) over the course of a life, especially with significant experiences.

01c0c24df44cda: Why normal people can do things they'd never imagine — conformity, obedience and the bystander effect, explained through the studies that discovered them.
00cf13cd8e6fbb:
You're not as much "yourself" as you think around others

Social psychology studies how the presence (real or imagined) of other people changes what we think, feel and do — sometimes in ways that would make us uncomfortable if we saw them coming.

Conformity: the Asch experiment

Solomon Asch showed a group of people lines of different lengths and asked them to pick which one matched a reference line — a trivial task. The trick: everyone except one real participant were actors instructed to deliberately give the OBVIOUSLY wrong answer.

📝 Result: about 75% of the real participants conformed with the group at least once, giving an answer they knew was wrong — just from the social pressure of not being the only one different.

Obedience: the Milgram experiment (revisited)

You already saw this in class 5: participants obeyed orders to deliver (supposedly) painful shocks to another person, just because an authority figure asked them to. They weren't "bad" people — they were ordinary people under situational pressure.

The bystander effect

The more people who witness an emergency, the less likely any one of them is to help — each one assumes "someone else" will act. This phenomenon, documented after the real 1964 case of Kitty Genovese, is called diffusion of responsibility.

💡 Practical application: if you ever need help in an emergency surrounded by people, point to ONE specific person ("You, in the blue jacket, call an ambulance") — breaking the diffusion of responsibility greatly increases the real odds of getting help.
⚠️ These studies don't say humans are "bad" by nature — they say the situation has more power than we usually believe, and that recognizing it is the first step to resisting it when it matters.

Where to go next

This course is an introduction — the starting point, not the end. If you really want to go deeper, here are real doors (not clickbait) to walk through:

  • A real introductory textbook (look up "Psychology" by David Myers, one of the most used university textbooks) will give you the depth this course could only hint at.
  • Serious YouTube and podcast content from psychologists with real training (not self-help coaches) on the specific topics that interested you most.
  • Observing your own life with this course's tools: when you notice you "conformed" with a group, that you conditioned a reaction, or that your memory "reconstructed" a memory — you're already thinking like a psychologist.
💡 One last reading tip: the curiosity you felt reading this is, by itself, the best predictor that you're going to keep learning psychology on your own — you don't need a course to require it of you.
